title: Orthodox Pascha
hookLine: at midnight: Christ is risen! Truly he is risen! and eggs dyed red for his blood

cards: "Christ is risen!" A priest shouts it at midnight from the doors of a church, and the crowd packed outside shouts back: "Truly he is risen!" He calls it again.
They answer again, in whatever language the parish prays. A little while ago the church was dark; now every hand holds a lit candle, and the bells are going. Old men shout it.
Children shout it louder. After the service, people go home to break the long fast, and on the table are eggs dyed deep red. Today, Orthodox Pascha.

teach.b: Paul writes, in the King James: "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us."
The Greek word behind passover there is pascha, the word Orthodox Christians use for Easter itself: the Passover of Christ, from death to life.
Luke says that on the first Easter evening, when two friends came back from Emmaus, the disciples met them with: "The Lord is risen indeed."
Pascha turns that into a greeting with two voices. One person says it, and someone else has to say it back; the news isn't finished until a second voice agrees.
Through the night the choir sings a short hymn again and again: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and giving life to those in the tombs. Not escaping death.
Walking through it and breaking it from the inside, the way the icon shows him standing on the broken gates. Then a sermon is read that tradition credits to John Chrysostom.
It invites everyone to the feast: those who kept the fast and those who didn't, those who came early and those who came at the last hour. Let no one fear death, it says. Then the eggs.
Tradition says the red is for the blood of Christ, and the shell is the sealed tomb that breaks open. A story people tell about Mary Magdalene and an egg that turned red isn't in the Gospels.
In some places people tap their eggs together, one saying Christ is risen, the other answering, to see whose cracks.

how: Orthodox Christians keep Pascha with a midnight service: the light passed from one candle, the greeting "Christ is risen!" answered "Truly he is risen!", and a meal afterward that breaks the fast, with eggs dyed red. The date can fall on a different Sunday from Western Easter.

games.q: the Paschal night — tap the pairs.

s: the sermon read at Pascha welcomes those who didn't keep the fast as well
it invites everyone: those who fasted and those who didn't, those who came early and those who came at the last hour.
the story of an egg turning red is told in the Gospels
it's a story people tell, not a Gospel story.
the Easter greeting needs only one voice
one calls, Christ is risen, and another answers, truly he is risen.

games.q: it's midnight. the priest turns to the crowd with his candle and calls out, Christ is risen! you're standing among them. what comes back?
games.why: the whole crowd shouts it back, again and again. the news isn't finished until a second voice agrees.

practice: Hold an egg, or any small, smooth thing, and mark it if you like, even with a pen: a cross. Feel the shell, closed and still, made to be broken open.
If you pray, say both halves of the greeting under your breath, Christ is risen, truly he is risen; if not, just hold it.

wordCard.voice: Orthodox Pascha. Easter as Orthodox Christians keep it: a midnight call of Christ is risen, the answer truly he is risen, and red eggs at the end of the fast.

orig.note: Greek: truly he is risen — the answer to Χριστὸς ἀνέστη, Christ is risen.

carryVoice: Your line: truly he is risen. From a bare altar, through the stations and the seven words, the broken gates, the fire and the dawn, to midnight: that was the week. See you tomorrow.
